subtitle: The minimum op-amp knowledge: golden rules, buffer, non-inverting amplifier
takeaways: Negative feedback: V_{+} = V_{-}, no input current
A buffer stops one stage loading the next
Check input and output range before any formula

slides.title: Op-amp and the golden rules
bullets: Amplifies the difference V_{+} − V_{-} with a huge gain A = 10^{5} … 10^{7}
Without feedback it is a comparator (flash ADC)
Negative feedback: part of V_{out} goes back to the inverting input
Rule 1: the output makes V_{+} = V_{-}; rule 2: inputs draw no current
slides.rule: V_{+} = V_{-}, I_{+} = I_{-} = 0 (with negative feedback)
slides.notes: With A = 10^{5} and 5 V out, the input difference is only 50 µV. Rule 1 holds only while the loop works: output not at a rail, feedback to the inverting input. Real inputs draw pA (CMOS) to some 10 nA (bipolar).

slides.title: Real op-amps on a single supply

left.head: CMOS rail-to-rail
bullets: Output within ~10 mV of the rails

right.head: Bipolar LM358
bullets: Inputs only up to V_{S} − 1.5 V

slides.notes: Most lab circuits run from 5 V or 12 V and ground. The input common-mode range and the output swing are the first things to check in every op-amp circuit; the golden rules only hold inside them. Output current is typically 10 … 40 mA, short-circuit protected.

slides.title: Loading and the voltage follower
bullets: Every connection: R_{out} of stage A and R_{in} of stage B form a divider
Follower: V_{out} = V_{in}, R_{in} → ∞ (GΩ … TΩ), R_{out} → 0
Stage A is not loaded, stage B sees an ideal source
slides.notes: Replace stage A by its Thevenin equivalent from chapter 1: a divider has R_{out} = R_{1}‖R_{2}. If R_{in} ≫ R_{out} cannot be met, put a buffer in between. Its load current comes from the supply, not from stage A.

slides.title: Falstad: buffering a potentiometer

falstad.name: buffer_pot
falstad.hint: Compare V_direct (0.714 V) with V_buffered (2.50 V)

observe: 10 kΩ pot at mid position: 2.5 V behind R_{out} = 2.5 kΩ
1 kΩ directly at the wiper collapses it; behind the follower: 2.50 V
Use the slider: how large must R_{L} be without a buffer?
slides.notes: The op-amp delivers 2.5 mA from the 5 V supply, the wiper delivers nothing. Without buffer R_{L} would need 250 kΩ for 1 % error. Exercise 2.1, including why an LM358 fails near 5 V.

slides.title: Falstad: two RC low-passes in cascade

falstad.name: buffer_rc_cascade
falstad.hint: Scope at f_{c} = 159 Hz: 0.500 V buffered vs 0.333 V direct

observe: With buffer: H = H_{1}·H_{2}, −6 dB at f_{c}
Directly connected: −9.5 dB, lower corner, softer knee
Buffered stages can be designed one by one (active filters)
slides.notes: Each stage is 10 kΩ and 100 nF. Without the buffer the second stage draws current from the first capacitor, so the product formula is no longer valid. This is the idea behind the chapter Active Filters.

slides.title: Non-inverting amplifier and buffer limits
bullets: R_{1}, R_{2} feed back part of V_{out}; R_{2} = 0 gives the follower
Gain set only by the resistor ratio: 1 % resistors → about 2 % gain error
Limits: output current, swing and input common-mode range
Capacitive load may oscillate: add 50 … 100 Ω in series with the output
slides.notes: Input resistance stays near infinite, so the source is still not loaded. Buffers appear behind references, at bridge taps, between filter stages and behind the hold capacitor. The chapter Operational Amplifiers derives the inverting amplifier and the effect of finite gain.
